draft.title: Cubic and quartic graphs
card: A factorised polynomial shows its x-intercepts. Set each bracket to zero. For y = (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3), the x-intercepts are x = −2, 1 and 3.
a bracket that appears once, such as (x − 1). The graph crosses the x-axis at that point.
a bracket that appears twice, such as (x − 1)². The graph touches the axis and turns back without crossing.
a bracket that appears three times, such as (x − 1)³. The graph flattens at the axis as it crosses.
draft.remember: Read the x-intercepts from the brackets. One factor crosses, a squared factor touches, a cubed factor flattens.

a.q: For y = (x − 4)²(x + 1), what does the graph do at x = 4?
opts: Touches the x-axis and turns back
Flattens as it crosses the x-axis
a.why: The factor (x − 4) is squared, so x = 4 is an x-intercept where the graph touches the axis and turns. A single factor would cross. A cubed factor would flatten as it crosses.
a.clue: Look at the power on the bracket (x − 4).

b.q: A graph is y = (x + 2)(x − 3)³. What does it do at x = 3 and at x = −2?
opts: Flattens as it crosses at x = 3, crosses at x = −2
Crosses at x = 3, flattens as it crosses at x = −2
Touches and turns at x = 3, crosses at x = −2
Flattens as it crosses at both x = 3 and x = −2
b.why: The bracket (x − 3) is cubed, so the graph flattens as it crosses at x = 3. The bracket (x + 2) appears once, so the graph simply crosses at x = −2. The powers belong to the brackets, not to the numbers inside them.
b.clue: Match each power to its own bracket, then set each bracket to zero.

a.best: Touches the x-axis and turns back

b.best: Flattens as it crosses at x = 3, crosses at x = −2
